questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The surgeon said the patient's condition was [critical] and moved her to the intensive care unit.
questions.explanation: In medicine 'critical' means very serious or dangerous; the move to intensive care confirms this. 'Stable' is the opposite idea.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The engineer warned that the building would collapse because its .......... was too shallow for the swampy soil.
questions.explanation: The foundation is the part of a building below ground that carries its load; only it can be described as too shallow for the soil.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The farmer applied .......... to the soil to replace the nutrients that the previous maize crop had removed.
questions.explanation: Fertiliser restores plant nutrients; pesticides, herbicides and fungicides kill pests, weeds and fungi respectively.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

When the company's profits fell, many investors sold their .......... and its price dropped sharply on the stock exchange.
questions.explanation: Shares are what investors buy and sell on the stock exchange; dividends are the profits paid on shares, and premiums belong to insurance.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

A .......... buys and sells shares on the stock exchange on behalf of clients.
questions.explanation: A stockbroker deals in shares for clients; an auctioneer sells goods to the highest bidder.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The nurse gave the baby an injection to .......... her against measles.
questions.explanation: To immunise is to protect against a disease, usually by vaccination; to diagnose is to identify a disease.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Because the disease is .........., the patients were kept in a separate ward away from visitors.
questions.explanation: Patients are isolated when a disease is contagious (spreads by contact). 'Chronic' means long-lasting and 'congenital' means present from birth; neither is a reason for isolation.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The government launched a tree-planting campaign to check the .......... that is turning farmland in the far north into sand.
questions.explanation: Desertification is the gradual change of fertile land into desert, which tree-planting (shelterbelts) is meant to check.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Before the festival began, the chief priest poured a .......... to the ancestors.
questions.explanation: A libation is a drink offering poured out in honour of ancestors or deities; homage and tribute are not poured.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The accused person was granted .......... on condition that he reported at the police station every Monday until his trial.
questions.explanation: Bail is temporary release of an accused person awaiting trial. Parole is early release of a convicted prisoner, so it does not fit someone not yet tried.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The court .......... the trader because there was no evidence linking him to the crime.
questions.explanation: To acquit is to declare a person not guilty; lack of evidence leads to acquittal, not conviction or sentence.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The driver was fined for .......... another vehicle on a sharp bend, where the road signs clearly forbade it.
questions.explanation: Overtaking means passing another vehicle; road signs forbid it on bends because the driver cannot see oncoming traffic.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Passengers were asked to fasten their seat belts as the aircraft began its .......... into Port Harcourt.
questions.explanation: An aircraft makes its descent as it comes down towards the destination airport; ascent and take-off happen at departure.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The Senate .......... the bill after its third reading and sent it to the President for assent.
questions.explanation: A bill that is passed goes to the President for assent; a rejected bill would not be sent, and the veto belongs to the President.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The council chairman presented the .........., showing how much the local government planned to spend in the coming year.
questions.explanation: A budget is a statement of planned income and spending; a manifesto states the promises of a party before an election.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The referee awarded a .......... after a defender handled the ball inside his own eighteen-yard box.
questions.explanation: A handball by a defender inside his own penalty area is punished with a penalty kick.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The new cathedral was .......... by the bishop at a colourful ceremony.
questions.explanation: A church building is consecrated (dedicated to sacred use); people, not buildings, are ordained, baptised or canonised.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The chemistry teacher made us repeat the .......... three times to be sure that our results were reliable.
questions.explanation: An experiment is the test that is carried out and repeated; a hypothesis is the idea it tests.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The technician advised us to .......... our files on an external drive in case the laptop crashed.
questions.explanation: To back up files is to keep extra copies so that they are not lost if the computer fails.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Every evening, Baba Sule drives his goats back into the .......... behind the house.
questions.explanation: A pen is an enclosure for goats or sheep; a sty is for pigs, a hive for bees and a kennel for dogs.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The company paid a popular musician to .......... its new brand of noodles in television advertisements.
questions.explanation: Celebrities endorse products by publicly recommending them in advertisements.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The principal's speech was so [verbose] that many students began to doze.
questions.explanation: Verbose means using more words than necessary, i.e. long-winded.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word in [brackets] and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

Tunde is usually [frugal] with his pocket money, but his brother is ..........
questions.explanation: Frugal means spending little; its opposite is extravagant (spending wastefully). Careful and prudent are near synonyms.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word in [brackets] and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

The new headmistress is [lenient] with latecomers, unlike her predecessor, who was ..........
questions.explanation: Lenient means not severe in punishing; the opposite is strict.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The witness's account of the accident was [lucid].
questions.explanation: Lucid means clear and easy to understand.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word in [brackets] and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

The minister's first remarks were [ambiguous], so journalists asked him to make his position ..........
questions.explanation: Ambiguous means open to more than one interpretation; unequivocal means clear and leaving no doubt.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The village has [scant] water during the dry season.
questions.explanation: Scant means barely enough or very little; 'plenty of' is its opposite.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem: In which of the following sentences is 'bank' used to mean the side of a river?
options: The fishermen pulled their canoe up onto the bank.
She paid the money into the bank on Monday.
You can bank on me to help you.
The pilot had to bank the plane to the left.
questions.explanation: Only the first sentence refers to the land along a river; the others use the homonym 'bank' (financial institution, rely on, tilt).

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The rescue team worked [tirelessly] after the building collapsed.
questions.explanation: Tirelessly means with great effort and without stopping to rest.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word in [brackets] and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

The reporter's account of the protest was [objective]; the editor's comment on it, however, was ..........
questions.explanation: Objective means not influenced by personal feelings; the opposite is biased.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The union leaders' attempt to [placate] the angry workers failed.
questions.explanation: To placate is to calm someone's anger, i.e. to pacify. Provoke is the opposite.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The new evidence [corroborated] the witness's statement.
questions.explanation: To corroborate is to confirm or support with fresh evidence.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word in [brackets] and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

Far from being [taciturn], the new prefect was quite ..........
questions.explanation: Taciturn means saying very little; garrulous means very talkative. Reserved and reticent are near synonyms of taciturn.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that is nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

After studying the report, the committee described the plan as [feasible].
questions.explanation: Feasible means possible to carry out, i.e. practicable.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

Mrs Okafor told her son to hold his horses before buying a car.
options: She told him to ride carefully.
She told him to sell his animals first.
She told him to save more money.
She told him to be patient.
questions.explanation: 'Hold your horses' means wait or be patient; it has nothing to do with real horses.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

Many staff feel that the new accountant is a square peg in a round hole.
options: He is not suited to his job.
He is new in the office.
questions.explanation: 'A square peg in a round hole' describes a person in a position that does not suit him.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

After the scandal, the councillor decided to face the music.
options: He accepted the consequences of his actions.
questions.explanation: To 'face the music' is to accept criticism or punishment for what one has done.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The two neighbours buried the hatchet after years of quarrelling.
questions.explanation: To 'bury the hatchet' is to end a quarrel and become friendly again.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

Musa always burns the midnight oil before his examinations.
options: He studies late into the night.
questions.explanation: To 'burn the midnight oil' is to work or study late at night.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The project was abandoned because the chairman got cold feet at the last minute.
options: He lost the courage to go ahead.
questions.explanation: To 'get cold feet' is to become nervous and lose the courage to do something planned.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The villagers took the contractor's promises with a pinch of salt.
questions.explanation: To take something 'with a pinch of salt' is to treat it with doubt or not believe it completely.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

After the fight in the dining hall, the principal read the riot act to the senior students.
options: He read them a law on public order.
questions.explanation: To 'read the riot act' is to warn someone sternly that they must stop behaving badly.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The thief was caught red-.......... with the stolen phone in his pocket.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is 'caught red-handed', i.e. caught in the act of doing wrong.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Throughout the trial, the young man .......... his innocence.
questions.explanation: 'Maintain one's innocence' is the normal collocation, meaning to keep insisting that one is innocent.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

Critics say the council only pays lip service to keeping the town clean.
options: It speaks loudly about the matter.
It spends a lot of money on it.
It refuses to discuss the matter.
It says it supports the idea but does little about it.
questions.explanation: To 'pay lip service' to something is to express support for it in words without acting on it.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The contractor's excuse for abandoning the road did not hold water.
questions.explanation: An argument that does not 'hold water' is not convincing or cannot be believed.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The police promised to leave no stone unturned in the search for the missing child.
options: They would dig up the area.
They would try every possible means.
They would search only the riverbank.
questions.explanation: To 'leave no stone unturned' is to try every possible way of finding or achieving something.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

Since the incident in the laboratory, Akin has been in the bad books of the chemistry teacher.
options: The teacher is displeased with him.
questions.explanation: To be 'in someone's bad books' is to be out of favour with that person.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The new coach was told that he would sink or swim with the team he had chosen.
options: He would have to teach the players to swim.
His success or failure would depend entirely on his own choice.
He would share the coaching with another person.
questions.explanation: 'Sink or swim' means to succeed or fail by one's own efforts, without help.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

If I .......... you, I would apologise to her at once.
questions.explanation: In unreal present conditions, formal English uses 'were' for all persons: 'If I were you, I would...'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

She told me that she .......... her homework the night before.
questions.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb, an action earlier than the reporting takes the past perfect: 'had done'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Each of the girls brought .......... own textbook to the lesson.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular and the antecedent is 'girls', so the matching possessive is 'her'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The committee has submitted .......... report to the principal.
questions.explanation: With the singular verb 'has', the committee is treated as one body, so the matching pronoun is 'its'. 'It's' means 'it is'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The young man was accused .......... stealing a goat.
questions.explanation: 'Accuse' takes the preposition 'of' (accused of stealing); 'charged with' is the other common pattern.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The principal congratulated the team .......... their victory in the quiz competition.
questions.explanation: Standard usage is 'congratulate someone on something'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Mrs Bello has been teaching in Kano .......... 2019.
questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with a point in time with the present perfect; 'for' is used with a period of time.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

By the time we arrived at the cinema, the film ..........
questions.explanation: The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect: 'had started'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

He would have passed the examination if he .......... harder.
questions.explanation: The third conditional pairs 'would have + past participle' with 'if + past perfect'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

I wish I .......... the answer when the teacher asked me yesterday.
questions.explanation: A wish about the past takes the past perfect: 'I wish I had known'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The man .......... car was stolen has reported the matter to the police.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' is the possessive relative pronoun: the man whose car was stolen.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The prize money was shared between Ade and ..........
questions.explanation: After the preposition 'between', the object form 'me' is required.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Ada is very good .......... mathematics.
questions.explanation: The standard collocation is 'good at' a subject or activity; 'good in' is a common error.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

It is high time we .......... for the motor park; the last bus leaves at six.
questions.explanation: 'It is high time' is followed by a past-tense form with present meaning: 'It is high time we left'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The suspect insisted that he .......... never seen the money before that day.
questions.explanation: After the past reporting verb 'insisted', the earlier experience is expressed with the past perfect 'had seen'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

This is the lady .......... I told you about yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Whom' is the object form of the relative pronoun for a person ('I told you about whom').

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The news of her son's admission to the university was music to Mama Bisi's ears.
options: She heard a song on the radio.
She could not hear the news.
questions.explanation: 'Music to one's ears' is a figurative way of saying something is very pleasant to hear.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

Our goalkeeper was a rock throughout the match.
options: He was unkind to the opponents.
questions.explanation: Calling someone 'a rock' figuratively means he was strong and reliable.

questions.stem: In which of the following sentences is 'cold' used figuratively?
options: The water in the clay pot is cold.
The visitors received a cold welcome from the villagers.
questions.explanation: A 'cold welcome' is unfriendly, not physically cold; the other sentences refer to actual temperature.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

Her friend's cruel words were a dagger in her heart.
options: Her friend threatened to stab her.
The words made her angry with everyone.
She did not care about the words.
questions.explanation: The metaphor compares the hurtful words to a dagger to show the deep emotional pain they caused.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The audit of the school's accounts opened a can of worms.
options: It found insects in the store.
questions.explanation: To 'open a can of worms' is to uncover a complicated set of problems that had been hidden.

questions.stem: In which of the following sentences is 'drowning' used figuratively?
options: The boy was drowning until a fisherman pulled him out.
Many animals drown during the floods.
Since he lost his job, Chidi has been drowning in debt.
The lifeguard saved a drowning tourist.
questions.explanation: One cannot literally drown in debt; it figuratively means having far more debt than one can manage.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The old man's memory is a library of our town's history.
options: He works in the town library.
He has forgotten the history of the town.
He knows a great deal about the history of the town.
questions.explanation: The metaphor compares his memory to a library to show how much historical knowledge it holds.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The opposition claimed that the government's economic plan was built on sand.
options: The plan was mainly about construction.
The plan was meant for desert areas.
The plan had no firm basis.
questions.explanation: Something 'built on sand' figuratively lacks a solid foundation and is likely to fail.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Neither the teacher nor the students .......... aware of the change in the timetable.
questions.explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject; 'students' is plural, so 'were'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The news from the hospital .......... not as bad as we had feared.
questions.explanation: 'News' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Mathematics .......... always been my favourite subject.
questions.explanation: Names of subjects ending in -ics, like 'mathematics', take a singular verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

You are coming with us to Enugu, ..........?
questions.explanation: A positive statement with 'are' takes the negative tag 'aren't you'. 'Isn't it' is a common error.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Let's go to the stadium early, ..........?
questions.explanation: The question tag for 'Let's ...' is 'shall we?'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

He hardly ever comes to class late, ..........?
questions.explanation: 'Hardly' makes the statement negative in meaning, so the tag is positive: 'does he?'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Of the two candidates for the post, Amaka is clearly the ..........
questions.explanation: When two people are compared, the comparative 'better' is used; 'more better' is a double comparative.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

This is the .......... result our school has ever recorded.
questions.explanation: 'Ever' compares this result with all others, so the superlative 'best' is required.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Both of the chief's .......... attended the ceremony.
questions.explanation: In the compound 'son-in-law', the main noun 'son' takes the plural: 'sons-in-law'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Kunle is one of the boys who .......... chosen to represent the state.
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'boys' (plural), so the verb is 'were'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The police .......... investigating the cause of the fire.
questions.explanation: 'Police' is a plural noun and takes a plural verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Hardly had we reached home .......... it started to rain.
questions.explanation: 'Hardly ... when' is the correct pair; 'than' goes with 'no sooner'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

No sooner had the bell rung .......... the students rushed out of the classroom.
questions.explanation: 'No sooner' is always followed by 'than'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

There isn't .......... sugar left in the tin.
questions.explanation: 'Sugar' is uncountable, so 'much' is used; 'many' and 'few' go with countable nouns.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Since he moved to Abuja, Femi has .......... friends; that is why he is often lonely.
questions.explanation: 'Few' (without 'a') means hardly any and fits the idea of loneliness; 'friends' is countable, so 'little' is wrong.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

I will attend the meeting .......... it rains, because it is very important.
questions.explanation: 'Even if' shows that the rain will not stop the speaker from going.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

You will fail the examination .......... you work harder.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not': you will fail if you do not work harder.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

.......... she was ill, Zainab came to school.
questions.explanation: 'Although' introduces a clause of contrast; 'despite' would need a noun phrase, e.g. 'Despite her illness'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

.......... the heavy rain, the match went on as planned.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is a preposition followed by a noun phrase ('the heavy rain'); 'although' and 'even though' need a clause.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Uche ran as fast as he could .......... catch the last bus.
questions.explanation: 'So as to' is followed by the infinitive; 'so that' and 'in order that' need a clause with a subject.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The .......... of the new bridge took two years.
questions.explanation: A noun is needed after 'the' as subject of the sentence: 'construction'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Her .......... to help others has won her many friends.
questions.explanation: A noun is needed after the possessive 'her': 'willingness'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The head girl spoke .......... at the assembly.
questions.explanation: An adverb is needed to modify the verb 'spoke': 'confidently'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Mr Eze .......... in this school for five years now.
questions.explanation: An action that began in the past and continues to the present ('for five years now') takes the present perfect.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The damaged roads .......... repaired before the rainy season begins.
questions.explanation: The passive with a modal is 'must be + past participle'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

She .......... her keys, so she cannot open the door now.
questions.explanation: The present perfect links a past action to its present result (she cannot open the door now).

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Not only .......... late, but he also forgot his books at home.
questions.explanation: When a sentence begins with 'Not only', the subject and auxiliary are inverted: 'Not only was he late...'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Seldom .......... such a brilliant performance by a junior student.
questions.explanation: A negative adverb such as 'seldom' at the start of a sentence causes inversion: 'Seldom have I seen'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The students, together with their teacher, .......... gone on an excursion to Yankari.
questions.explanation: 'Together with their teacher' does not change the subject, which is the plural 'the students'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Either Ngozi or her sisters .......... cooking tonight.
questions.explanation: With 'either ... or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'sisters', so it is plural.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Twenty kilometres .......... a long distance to walk in the sun.
questions.explanation: A plural expression of distance thought of as a single amount takes a singular verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The officer asked me where ..........
questions.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order and backshift of tense: 'where I lived'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

At the wedding, Funke wore a .......... dress.
questions.explanation: Adjectives normally follow the order opinion, size, colour, material: beautiful long red silk.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Chinedu prefers rice .......... yam.
questions.explanation: 'Prefer' is followed by 'to' when comparing two things: prefer rice to yam.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The economic .......... facing many countries have affected prices in our markets.

Washing hands with soap is a cheap and simple way of preventing many diseases.

potholes, traders and the high cost of fuel
traffic lights that do not work

tailoring is the most useful trade for students
students should leave school to learn a trade

The rainy season has become longer than before.
Flooding in our towns is largely caused by residents' own habits.
Houses built on waterways are very expensive.

Every harvest season, the tomato sellers in the main market of a small town near Kano watched helplessly as a large part of their stock turned soft and sour within days. Halima Sani, who had grown up helping her mother at a vegetable stall there, knew the problem only too well. After studying agricultural engineering at a polytechnic, she came home with an idea that many of the traders at first dismissed as a dream.

She pooled her savings with a small grant from a women's cooperative and built a cold room powered by solar panels at one end of the market. Traders could store their crates there for a modest daily fee, paid in naira or, for the poorest, in a few baskets of produce. Within a year, the losses that had once eaten up half of every trader's profit had fallen sharply.

The traders who had laughed now queued at her door before sunrise. Some of them, she admits, still grumble about the fee, but none of them wants to go back to the old days. "People do not resist change," she says. "They resist losing what little they have. Show them that change protects what they have, and they will run towards it."

Halima's success has not come without problems. Thieves once stole two of her panels, and the dusty harmattan wind forces her to clean the rest every morning. Yet she speaks of these difficulties lightly, as if they were simply part of the day's work. Her next plan is to train young people from nearby villages to build similar rooms, so that farmers can keep their produce fresh before it even reaches the town.

What problem did the tomato sellers face before the cold room was built?
options: Much of their produce spoilt within a few days.
Thieves stole their crates every night.
They paid very high taxes to the market.
questions.explanation: The first sentence says much of their stock turned soft and sour within days.

When the old community library in our town closed for lack of funds, few people seemed to notice. Its shelves had long been filled with yellowing books that nobody borrowed, and the reading room was more often used as a quiet place to sleep than to study. It was Mr Adebayo Ojo, a retired headmaster, who refused to let it die.

He began by asking every family he knew to donate one book their children had outgrown. Within three months, the pile of donations had grown so large that he had to borrow shelves from a nearby church. He then persuaded two young graduates doing their national service in the town to run reading sessions every Saturday morning.

The early sessions were poorly attended. Children used to the bright screens of their parents' phones found the printed page dull. Mr Ojo did not scold them. Instead, he read aloud the most exciting parts of adventure stories and stopped just before the end, leaving the children to find out for themselves what happened next. It was, he admits with a smile, a small trick, but it worked. By the end of the year, the reading room was so crowded on Saturdays that latecomers sat on mats in the corridor.

Today the library is run by a committee of parents, and the local government has promised to pay for electricity and repairs. Mr Ojo still comes every Saturday, though he now prefers to listen rather than to read. "A child who reads," he likes to say, "will never be a stranger anywhere in the world."

Why did the old community library close?
options: The church took over its shelves.
questions.explanation: The first sentence says it closed "for lack of funds".

questions.stem:
Your friend who lives abroad has asked you how your community celebrates its most important annual festival. Write a letter to him or her describing the festival as it was celebrated this year.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — name and purpose of the festival; preparations; main events in order (e.g. procession, masquerades or durbar, dances, feasting); the role of different groups (elders, youths, women); what made this year special; personal feelings
10 marks: Organisation — writer's address and date; no inside address; informal salutation (e.g. Dear Tobi); introduction with greetings and purpose; well-arranged paragraphs; conclusion with good wishes; informal close (e.g. Your friend), first name only
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: An informal letter opening with warm greetings and a reference to the friend's request. The body names the festival (e.g. a new yam festival), explains its origin and meaning, then describes the preparations, the opening rites by the elders, the procession, the masquerades and dances, the feasting and the visitors who came home for it, and mentions something new this year (e.g. a cultural competition for schools). It closes with an invitation to attend next year, regards to the friend's family, 'Your friend' and the first name.

10 marks: Organisation — writer's address and date; inside address (The Chairman, ... Local Government Area); 'Dear Sir/Madam'; a suitable heading (e.g. THE DEPLORABLE STATE OF ... ROAD); paragraphed body with clear introduction and conclusion; 'Yours faithfully', signature and full name
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: A formal letter with both addresses, 'Dear Sir' and a heading. The writer introduces himself as a student of the school and states his purpose, describes the deep potholes and gullies and the flooding after rain, explains the consequences (students arriving late and muddy, a recent motorcycle accident, commercial drivers refusing to ply the road or doubling fares), then suggests urgent repairs, proper drains and regular maintenance, offering community cooperation. It ends politely, expressing confidence that the chairman will act, with 'Yours faithfully' and full name.

questions.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

Ifeoma had never been afraid of words. At home in Onitsha she read everything she could find: old newspapers, the labels on her mother's provision boxes, even the instructions on medicine packets. So when her English teacher entered her for the state spelling competition, everyone, including Ifeoma herself, expected her to do well.

What nobody expected was the hall. It was enormous, its ceiling lost somewhere above rows of bright lights, and it was packed with students, teachers and parents from every corner of the state. When Ifeoma climbed onto the stage and saw the sea of faces before her, her mouth turned to sand. The first word she was given was one she had spelt correctly a hundred times. She opened her mouth, and nothing came out.

The judge, a kindly woman with silver hair, repeated the word slowly. Ifeoma closed her eyes. Suddenly she remembered her grandmother, who had sold pepper in the market for forty years and who had never once been to school. "When the crowd is too big," her grandmother used to say, "talk to one person. The rest will listen anyway." Ifeoma opened her eyes, found the face of a small boy in the front row who was swinging his legs, and spelt the word to him, letter by letter.

She did not win. A tall boy from Awka, who spelt words that most of the adults in the hall had never heard of, took the trophy home. But Ifeoma reached the final round, and when she walked off the stage, her teacher was beaming as though she had won. On the bus home, Ifeoma thought less about the words she had missed than about the small boy in the front row. She had learnt something that day that no dictionary could have taught her.

(a) Give two pieces of evidence from the passage which show that Ifeoma loved reading. [2 marks]
(b) What happened to Ifeoma when she first saw the audience? [2 marks]
(c) What advice had Ifeoma's grandmother given, and how did Ifeoma use it? [2 marks]
(d) Why was Ifeoma's teacher "beaming as though she had won"? [2 marks]
(e) What do you think Ifeoma learnt "that no dictionary could have taught her"? [2 marks]
(f) "who had sold pepper in the market for forty years" (i) What grammatical name is given to this expression? (ii) What is its function? [2 marks]
(g) "her mouth turned to sand" (i) What figure of speech is used here? (ii) What does it mean? [2 marks]
(h) For each of the following words, find another word or phrase which means the same and which can replace it as it is used in the passage: (i) enormous (ii) packed (iii) kindly (iv) final (v) beaming (vi) expected [6 marks]

2 marks: (b) she was overcome by fear; her mouth went dry and she could not speak / could not spell a word she knew well
2 marks: (c) advice: when the crowd is too big, talk to one person (1); she fixed her eyes on a small boy in the front row and spelt the word to him (1)
2 marks: (d) the teacher was proud of her / pleased that she overcame her fear and reached the final round

questions.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

Along the coast of the Niger Delta, where the rivers meet the sea, stretch some of the largest mangrove forests in Africa. To a visitor travelling by boat, they may look like nothing more than a tangle of twisted roots rising out of muddy water. Yet these forests are among the most valuable ecosystems on earth.

The mangrove's roots, which arch above the water like the legs of a giant spider, slow down the movement of the tides. In doing so, they trap mud and protect the shoreline from being washed away. During storms they act as a natural wall, absorbing the force of the waves before it reaches the villages behind them.

Beneath the water, the roots serve another purpose. They provide shelter for young fish, crabs, shrimps and periwinkles, which hide among them until they are big enough to survive in open water. Fishermen in the delta know this well: where the mangroves are healthy, the catch is plentiful; where they have been cut down, the nets come up nearly empty.

Unfortunately, the mangroves are disappearing. Some are cut for firewood and building poles, some are cleared to make way for new settlements, and others are destroyed by oil spills that coat the roots and suffocate the trees. Once a mangrove forest is lost, it can take decades to recover, if it recovers at all.

There are, however, signs of hope. In several communities, young people have begun replanting mangrove seedlings along damaged creeks, and some schools now take pupils on boat trips to show them why these forests matter. The task is enormous, but as one elderly fisherman put it, "The mangrove fed my father and it fed me. If we look after it, it will feed our grandchildren too."

(a) Why might a visitor fail to see the value of the mangrove forests? [2 marks]
(b) State two ways in which mangroves protect the coastline. [2 marks]
(c) How do the mangroves help fishermen? [2 marks]
(d) Mention two causes of the loss of mangroves. [2 marks]
(e) What does the elderly fisherman's statement reveal about his attitude to the mangroves? [2 marks]
(f) "where the mangroves are healthy" (i) What grammatical name is given to this expression? (ii) What is its function? [2 marks]
(g) "which arch above the water like the legs of a giant spider" (i) What figure of speech is used here? (ii) What does it tell us about the roots? [2 marks]
(h) For each of the following words, find another word or phrase which means the same and which can replace it as it is used in the passage: (i) tangle (ii) valuable (iii) shelter (iv) plentiful (v) suffocate (vi) enormous [6 marks]

2 marks: (a) to a visitor they look like nothing more than a tangle of twisted roots in muddy water
2 marks: (b) any two: they slow down the tides / they trap mud and stop the shore being washed away / they act as a natural wall absorbing the force of storm waves
2 marks: (c) the roots shelter young fish, crabs, shrimps and periwinkles until they grow, so the catch is plentiful where mangroves are healthy
2 marks: (d) any two: cutting for firewood and building poles / clearing for new settlements / oil spills
2 marks: (e) he values them deeply as a lasting source of livelihood for generations and believes they must be protected

2 marks: (g) (i) simile (1); (ii) the roots are long and curve up and out of the water (1)
6 marks: (h) one mark each: (i) mass / jumble / mesh (ii) precious / useful (iii) protection / refuge / hiding place (iv) abundant / large (v) choke / kill (by cutting off air) (vi) huge / very great

(c) They shelter young fish and other sea creatures, so fishermen catch more. (d) Cutting for firewood and poles; oil spills. (e) He values them as a source of food for past and future generations and wants them protected. (f) Adverbial clause of place modifying 'is'. (g) Simile: the roots are long and curved like a spider's legs. (h) jumble; precious; refuge; abundant; choke; huge.

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

The night bus from Lagos was supposed to reach Jos by seven in the morning. At about two o'clock, on a lonely stretch of road far from any town, the engine coughed twice and died. The driver, a short man who had said nothing since we left the park, climbed down with a torch and disappeared under the bonnet. The rest of us sat in the darkness and listened to the crickets.

At first, nobody spoke. Strangers on a night bus have an unwritten agreement to leave one another alone. But as the minutes became an hour, the silence began to break. A trader with a basket of dried fish wondered aloud whether armed robbers used this road. A young mother hushed her crying baby and told him, rather sharply, to keep such thoughts to himself. An old man in a faded agbada laughed and said he had travelled this road for thirty years and had met nothing more dangerous than a goat.

Then the driver returned. The fan belt had snapped, he announced, and he had no spare. A groan rose from every seat. It was the old man who found a way out. He asked whether anyone had a strong piece of cloth, and when a nurse produced a long strip of thick bandage from her bag, he and the driver twisted it into a temporary belt. "It will not take us to Jos," the old man warned, "but it will take us to the next town."

It did. By dawn we were drinking hot tea at a roadside canteen while a mechanic fitted a new belt. The trader shared his fish, the young mother let the nurse hold her baby, and the old man told stories of his travels until we forgot how tired we were. I have made many journeys since then, but I have never again felt that strangers on a bus were simply strangers.

(a) What caused the bus to stop? [2 marks]
(b) What does the writer mean by "Strangers on a night bus have an unwritten agreement to leave one another alone"? [2 marks]
(c) Why did the young mother speak sharply to the trader? [2 marks]
(d) How did the old man solve the problem? [2 marks]
(e) How had the relationship among the passengers changed by the morning? [2 marks]
(f) "as the minutes became an hour" (i) What grammatical name is given to this expression? (ii) What is its function? [2 marks]
(g) "the engine coughed twice and died" (i) What figure of speech is used here? (ii) What does it mean? [2 marks]
(h) For each of the following words, find another word or phrase which means the same and which can replace it as it is used in the passage: (i) lonely (ii) disappeared (iii) faded (iv) announced (v) temporary (vi) shared [6 marks]

2 marks: (b) passengers who do not know one another usually keep to themselves and do not talk, though nobody has stated this as a rule
2 marks: (c) his talk of armed robbers was frightening the passengers / she did not want fear spread among them
2 marks: (d) he and the driver twisted a strip of bandage provided by a nurse into a temporary fan belt
2 marks: (e) they became friendly and shared things / they no longer felt like strangers to one another
2 marks: (f) (i) adverbial clause of time (1); (ii) it modifies the verb "began" (1)
2 marks: (g) (i) personification (1); (ii) the engine made spluttering noises and then stopped working (1)

(d) He twisted a nurse's bandage into a temporary fan belt with the driver. (e) They became friendly, sharing food, care of the baby and stories. (f) Adverbial clause of time modifying 'began'. (g) Personification: the engine spluttered and stopped. (h) deserted; vanished; worn; declared; makeshift; distributed.

questions.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

Many secondary school students believe that the surest way to pass an examination is to sleep as little as possible in the weeks before it. They stay awake until the early hours, drinking strong coffee to keep their eyes open, and boast to their friends about how few hours they have slept. Scientists who study the brain, however, have reached a very different conclusion.

Sleep, they explain, is not wasted time. While we sleep, the brain sorts through the information it has received during the day, storing what is important and discarding what is not. A student who has read three chapters of biology in the evening will remember more of them the next morning if he sleeps well than if he stays up reading a fourth chapter. In other words, sleep is the time when learning is fixed in the memory.

Lack of sleep also affects concentration. A tired student reads the same paragraph several times without understanding it, makes careless mistakes in calculations and is easily irritated. Over a long period, too little sleep weakens the body's defences against illness, so that the student who has worked hardest may fall sick just as the examination begins.

None of this means that students should sleep all day. The point is balance. Experts generally advise teenagers to sleep for about eight to ten hours a night, to go to bed and wake up at regular times, and to put away phones and other screens some time before sleeping, since the light from them can keep the brain alert. A student who follows this advice may find that he studies for fewer hours but learns more in each of them.

The next time a friend boasts of studying all night, it may be worth asking a simple question: how much of what you read can you remember?

(a) What do many students believe about preparing for examinations? [2 marks]
(b) According to the passage, what does the brain do while we sleep? [2 marks]
(c) State two ways in which lack of sleep affects a student's work. [2 marks]
(d) Why might a hardworking student fall ill just as the examination begins? [2 marks]
(e) What is the writer's purpose in the last paragraph? [2 marks]
(f) "if he sleeps well" (i) What grammatical name is given to this expression? (ii) What is its function? [2 marks]
(g) "how much of what you read can you remember?" (i) What literary device is this? (ii) Why does the writer use it? [2 marks]
(h) For each of the following words, find another word or phrase which means the same and which can replace it as it is used in the passage: (i) surest (ii) boast (iii) discarding (iv) fixed (v) irritated (vi) alert [6 marks]

2 marks: (d) long-term lack of sleep weakens the body's defences against illness
2 marks: (e) to make the reader question the habit of studying all night / to persuade students that what matters is how much they remember, not how long they read
2 marks: (f) (i) adverbial clause of condition (1); (ii) it modifies the verb (phrase) "will remember" (1)

(c) The student cannot understand what he reads and makes careless mistakes. (d) Lack of sleep over a long time weakens the body's resistance to illness. When Obinna's father announced that his son would spend the long vacation at Mazi Okeke's workshop, Obinna was horrified. He had imagined spending the holidays playing football and watching films, not lying on his back under dusty cars. But his father's decision, like the sun rising in the east, was not open to discussion.

The workshop stood beside a busy road in Aba: a patch of oily ground under a rusty zinc roof, surrounded by the skeletons of vehicles that would never move again. Mazi Okeke was a tall, silent man whose hands were permanently stained black. On the first day he gave Obinna a broom and pointed at the floor. On the second day he did the same, and on the third. By the end of the week, Obinna was convinced that he had been sent there as a cleaner.

On the eighth day, a woman drove in with a car that refused to start. Mazi Okeke listened to the engine for a moment and then, without looking up, asked Obinna which spanner he would need. To his own surprise, Obinna knew. For a whole week, while he swept, he had been watching: which tools the apprentices reached for, where they were kept, how the older boys handled each part. His master, it turned out, had been teaching him all along.

From then on the lessons came quickly. Obinna learnt to change oil and fit brake pads, and to tell from the sound of an engine whether its trouble was serious. He also learnt things that were harder to name: to listen before speaking, to finish one job before starting another, and to treat every customer, rich or poor, with the same respect.

When school resumed, his classmates noticed that he had grown quieter. He no longer rushed through his mathematics homework, and when he did not know an answer, he watched, waited and worked it out. His father said nothing, but he smiled a great deal that term.

(a) Why was Obinna horrified by his father's decision? [2 marks]
(b) Give two details that describe Mazi Okeke's workshop. [2 marks]
(c) Why did Obinna think he had been sent to the workshop as a cleaner? [2 marks]
(d) What did Obinna discover on the eighth day? [2 marks]
(e) Mention two lessons Obinna learnt that had nothing to do with repairing cars. [2 marks]

(g) "like the sun rising in the east" (i) What figure of speech is used here? (ii) What does it tell us about the father's decision? [2 marks]
(h) For each of the following words, find another word or phrase which means the same and which can replace it as it is used in the passage: (i) horrified (ii) permanently (iii) convinced (iv) resumed (v) rushed (vi) handled [6 marks]

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

Not long ago, a farmer in a remote village who wanted to send money to a son studying in the city had few choices. He could travel to the nearest town with a bank, often a journey of several hours, or he could give the cash to a lorry driver and hope that it arrived. Today, in many such villages, he simply walks to a small kiosk at the junction, where an agent sends the money in minutes using a mobile phone.

These agents have become an important part of rural life. Most of them are ordinary traders who added the service to their existing businesses. They accept cash deposits, pay out withdrawals and help customers to buy airtime or pay for electricity. Because they live in the community, they know their customers by name, and many villagers who would never walk into a bank feel comfortable dealing with them.

The benefits are clear. Farmers can receive payment for their crops without carrying large sums of cash along dangerous roads. Market women can save small amounts regularly instead of hiding money under their mattresses, where it may be stolen or eaten by rats. Families in the city can send help quickly when a relative falls ill.

The system is not without its problems, however. Network failures sometimes leave customers stranded for hours, and dishonest people have found ways to trick the unwary, for example by sending false messages claiming that money has been paid. Some agents also run short of cash on market days, when demand is highest.

Even so, few villagers would wish to return to the old days. As one agent remarked, "Before, money travelled like a tortoise. Now it travels like lightning. Our work is to make sure it also travels safely."

(a) In what two ways did a village farmer send money in the past? [2 marks]
(b) Who are the agents, and what services do they provide? [2 marks]
(c) Why do many villagers prefer dealing with agents to going to a bank? [2 marks]
(d) State two benefits of the agents' service mentioned in the passage. [2 marks]
(e) Mention two problems of the system. [2 marks]
(f) "who would never walk into a bank" (i) What grammatical name is given to this expression? (ii) What is its function? [2 marks]
(g) "money travelled like a tortoise" (i) What figure of speech is used here? (ii) What does it mean? [2 marks]
(h) For each of the following words, find another word or phrase which means the same and which can replace it as it is used in the passage: (i) remote (ii) existing (iii) regularly (iv) stranded (v) unwary (vi) remarked [6 marks]

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

Few problems trouble our education system as much as examination malpractice. Every year, results are withheld, candidates are barred and some centres are derecognised because of cheating. To deal with the problem, we must first understand why it happens.

The first cause lies in the value that society places on certificates. Many employers look only at the grades a candidate presents, not at what he can actually do, so young people come to believe that the paper matters more than the knowledge it is supposed to represent. Closely related to this is the fear of failure. A student who knows that his parents have sold goods or borrowed money to pay his fees may feel that he cannot afford to fail, whatever it takes.

Poor preparation is another cause. Some students spend the school year on social media, parties and other distractions, and remember their books only when the examination is a few weeks away. By then it is too late to learn honestly what should have been learnt over three years.

Finally, there are adults who profit from cheating. Some so-called "special centres" charge candidates large sums of money with the promise of guaranteed success, and a few dishonest officials sell question papers before examinations.

What, then, can be done? Parents and teachers must begin by teaching children that knowledge, not paper, is the true reward of education, and that an honest failure is better than a dishonest pass. Above all, those who aid and abet cheating, whether owners of special centres or corrupt officials, should be prosecuted and punished publicly, so that others are deterred.

(a) In four sentences, one for each, summarise the causes of examination malpractice. [20 marks]
(b) In two sentences, one for each, summarise the measures the writer suggests for dealing with it. [10 marks]

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

Walk along almost any street in our cities after a heavy rain and you will see the same sight: plastic bottles, nylon bags and food packs piled up in gutters and floating in pools of dirty water. Plastic has made life convenient in many ways, but the careless way we dispose of it has created serious problems.

The most visible of these is flooding. Plastic bags and bottles block drains and culverts, so that rainwater which should flow away spreads into streets and homes instead. Each year, families lose property, and sometimes lives, in floods made worse by rubbish that they or their neighbours threw away.

Plastic waste is also a threat to health. Bottles and containers that collect rainwater become breeding places for mosquitoes, which spread malaria. When heaps of refuse are burnt, as often happens, the smoke releases harmful chemicals into the air that people breathe.

Animals suffer too. Goats and cows that roam the streets often swallow nylon bags along with scraps of food, and many die slowly as the plastic blocks their stomachs. In the sea and the lagoons, fish and turtles become trapped in plastic, and tiny pieces of broken-down plastic find their way into the fish that we later eat.

Plastic waste also spoils the beauty of our environment. Streets lined with rubbish discourage tourists and investors and give visitors a poor impression of a town, however rich its history or culture.

Fortunately, the problem is not beyond solution. Households can sort their waste and sell plastic bottles to the recycling companies whose collectors now visit many neighbourhoods, earning a little money while keeping the streets clean. Governments, for their part, should enforce existing laws against dumping refuse in drains and provide enough waste bins and regular collection, so that citizens have no excuse for throwing rubbish anywhere they like.

(a) In four sentences, one for each, summarise the problems caused by plastic waste. [20 marks]
(b) In two sentences, one for each, summarise the solutions suggested by the writer. [10 marks]

5 marks: (b)(ii) Governments should enforce anti-dumping laws and provide bins and regular collection. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)

When Kemi's parents asked her whether she wanted to attend a boarding school or remain at home and go to the day school in her neighbourhood, she asked for a week to think about it. She spoke to her cousin, who had just finished six years in a boarding school, and she listened carefully.

Her cousin was full of praise for boarding life. Living in school, she said, teaches a young person to be independent. There is no mother to wake you up, wash your clothes or remind you to do your homework, so you quickly learn to manage your own affairs. She also pointed out that boarders have more time for their studies. Since they do not spend hours in traffic every morning and evening, they can attend organised prep in the evenings, when teachers are often on hand to help them.

The cousin added that boarding school brings together students from different parts of the country. She had shared a room with girls who spoke four different languages at home, and she had learnt to respect customs very different from her own; some of those girls were now her closest friends. She also mentioned the many activities available after classes, from drama and debating to football and the school band, which help students to discover talents they never knew they had.

But her cousin was honest about the difficulties as well. The food, she admitted with a laugh, was rarely as good as food at home, and in her first year she had often gone to bed hungry. More seriously, being far from home means that parents cannot easily guide their children through difficult moments. A child who is bullied or who falls into bad company may suffer for weeks before anyone at home finds out.

Kemi thought about all this for the whole week. In the end, she chose the boarding school, but she asked her parents for one promise: that they would come on every visiting day.

(a) In four sentences, one for each, summarise the advantages of boarding school mentioned by Kemi's cousin. [20 marks]
(b) In two sentences, one for each, summarise the disadvantages she mentioned. [10 marks]

5 marks: (a)(iv) After-class activities help students to discover their talents. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)

Agriculture employs a large proportion of Nigerians, and most of the food we eat is grown not on huge plantations but on small family farms. Yet the men and women who work these farms face difficulties that would discourage people in almost any other occupation.

The first of these is lack of money. Most small farmers cannot obtain loans from banks, which demand collateral that they do not possess, so they cannot afford improved seeds, fertiliser or machines. They continue to farm with hoes and cutlasses, as their grandparents did, and their yields remain low.

Secondly, many farms are far from good roads. After harvest, farmers must carry their produce on their heads or on motorcycles along bush paths to reach a market, and much of it is damaged on the way. Those who cannot reach a market are forced to sell to middlemen who come to the village and pay whatever price they choose.

Storage is a third problem. Without silos, cold rooms or even simple dry stores, farmers must sell their crops immediately after harvest, when prices are at their lowest, instead of waiting until prices rise.

Fourthly, small farmers are at the mercy of the weather. Rains that arrive late or stop early can destroy a whole season's work, and few farmers have irrigation or insurance to protect them.

These problems are serious, but they are not hopeless. Farmers who join cooperatives can pool their resources, obtain loans as a group and buy inputs more cheaply. Government and private investors, for their part, can build rural roads and storage facilities, which would allow farmers to sell their produce in good condition and at fair prices.

(a) In four sentences, one for each, summarise the problems facing small farmers. [20 marks]
(b) In two sentences, one for each, summarise the solutions the writer proposes. [10 marks]

5 marks: (a)(ii) Poor roads cause damage to produce and force them to sell cheaply to middlemen. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (a)(iii) Lack of storage forces them to sell at harvest when prices are lowest. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (a)(iv) They depend on unreliable weather, without irrigation or insurance. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (b)(i) Farmers should form cooperatives to get loans and buy inputs cheaply. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (b)(ii) Government and private investors should build rural roads and storage facilities. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)

Lack of storage forces them to sell cheaply at harvest. Unreliable weather can ruin their crops. (b) Farmers should form cooperatives. Government and investors should provide roads and storage.

Drug abuse among young people has become a matter of national concern. Health workers report that more and more teenagers are taking substances such as codeine cough syrups, tramadol and cannabis, often without fully understanding what these do to the body and mind.

Many begin out of curiosity or because their friends are doing it. In a group where everyone seems to be taking something, the young person who refuses may be laughed at or left out, and few teenagers have the confidence to stand alone. Others turn to drugs to escape problems at home, such as quarrels between parents, or the stress of school and unemployment.

The effects of drug abuse are grave. Physically, many of these substances damage vital organs such as the liver, kidneys and brain, and an overdose can kill. Mentally, users may suffer anxiety, depression or even serious mental illness, and some end up in psychiatric hospitals. Drug abuse also wrecks education and careers: users lose concentration, miss classes or work and eventually drop out. Finally, the habit often leads to crime. A young person who needs money for drugs may begin by stealing from his own family and end by joining gangs that rob strangers.

The fight against drug abuse must begin at home. Parents who spend time with their children, talk to them openly and notice changes in their behaviour are far better placed to protect them than parents who are always too busy. Schools and religious bodies also have a part to play, by teaching young people the facts about drugs and helping them to build the confidence to say no, whatever their friends may think.

(a) In four sentences, one for each, summarise the effects of drug abuse on young people. [20 marks]
(b) In two sentences, one for each, summarise the ways of fighting drug abuse suggested in the passage. [10 marks]

(b) Parents should be close to their children and watch their behaviour. Schools and religious bodies should educate young people and help them say no.

In the past few years, a growing number of young Nigerians have enrolled in courses on computer programming, graphic design, digital marketing and other technology skills. Training centres have opened in many cities, and some young people learn entirely online, using free videos and tutorials on their phones.

Several reasons explain this trend. The most obvious is employment. Jobs in offices and the public service are limited, and many graduates wait for years without finding one. Digital skills open a different door: a young person who can design a website or manage a company's online advertising can find work without waiting for a vacancy to be advertised.

Another attraction is that much of this work can be done from anywhere. A programmer in Owerri can work for a company in Lagos, or even for a client on another continent, without leaving home. This allows young people to earn while remaining close to their families, and some earn far more than they could in local jobs.

The low cost of starting is a third reason. Unlike many businesses, which require a shop, stock or heavy equipment, a digital business may need little more than a laptop, an internet connection and skill. Finally, the success of several Nigerian technology companies, some of which have attracted international investment, has inspired many young people to believe that they too can build something new.

There are, however, obstacles. Electricity supply remains unreliable in many areas, so people who work online must spend heavily on generators, fuel or solar systems. The cost of data and devices is also high for young people who are just starting out, and some promising learners give up because they cannot afford them.

(a) In four sentences, one for each, summarise the reasons why many young Nigerians are learning digital skills. [20 marks]
(b) In two sentences, one for each, summarise the obstacles they face. [10 marks]

5 marks: (a)(i) Formal jobs are scarce, and digital skills offer employment. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (a)(ii) Digital work can be done from anywhere. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (a)(iii) A digital business costs little to start. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (a)(iv) The success of Nigerian technology companies inspires them. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (b)(i) Electricity supply is unreliable and alternatives are costly. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (b)(ii) Data and devices are expensive. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
questions.explanation: (a) Digital skills provide work when office jobs are scarce. The work can be done from anywhere. Starting a digital business is cheap. Successful local tech companies inspire young people. (b) Power supply is unreliable. Data and devices are costly.
